questions.q: Which ordering lists the layers you rely on in everyday computer use from **top (closest to you) to bottom**?
choices: Applications → operating system → hardware → physical components
Operating system → applications → hardware → physical components
Applications → hardware → operating system → physical components
Hardware → operating system → applications → physical components
questions.explain: You run **applications** (written by other programmers) that run on an **OS** (written by other developers) that runs on **hardware** (built by other manufacturers) made of **physical components** (metal, plastic, electricity). Each layer depends on the one below it.

questions.q: Which statement best captures **abstraction** as used in this lesson?
choices: Hiding how something works behind a simpler interface so its user only needs to know *what* it does
Writing code without comments so it is harder to reverse-engineer
Translating a high-level language directly into electricity
Replacing hardware with software emulation
questions.explain: Abstraction hides the *how* behind an interface that exposes the *what*. Each layer of the stack gives the layer above a simplified view: applications see files and windows, not disk sectors; the OS sees "a CPU that executes instructions," not transistor layouts.

questions.q: If abstraction lets millions of people use computers without knowing the internals, why study the lower layers at all?
choices: When something breaks, runs slowly, or must be secured, the explanation usually lives in a lower layer
Because the upper layers are going away and will be replaced by hardware
Because applications cannot run unless the user understands the hardware
Because abstraction is an insult to programmers
questions.explain: "Superficial" is not an insult: abstraction is what makes computers usable. The catch is that bugs, performance problems and security holes are usually explained by what happens *underneath*, which is what a systems course teaches.

questions.q: You drag a file into a folder in File Explorer. What actually decides which disk blocks get updated?
choices: The operating system's file-system code, which File Explorer asks to make the change
File Explorer itself, which writes directly to the SSD's blocks
The SSD, which reorganizes folders on its own when a file is moved
The CPU's ALU
questions.explain: File Explorer is only an **application** that *shows* the file system. It asks the OS (via system calls) to make the change, and the OS's **file system** (NTFS, ext4, APFS…) maps named files and directories onto raw numbered storage blocks and updates metadata.

questions.q: A file system is the scheme the OS uses to organize raw, numbered storage blocks into named files inside a tree of directories, including metadata such as sizes, timestamps and permissions.
questions.explain: Physically a drive is just a huge array of fixed-size blocks. The file system (NTFS, APFS, ext4, FAT32/exFAT) is the OS-level organization that turns those blocks into files, folders and metadata.

questions.q: Which pairing of layer and "what it sees" is correct?
choices: Application: files, windows and network connections
Application: disk sectors and radio signals
Operating system: the internal layout of transistors
Hardware designer: HTTP requests
questions.explain: An application sees high-level abstractions (files, windows, connections). The OS sees a CPU, addressable memory and device controllers, but not transistor layout. The hardware designer works with gates built from transistors.

questions.q: Which of these are jobs of an **operating system**?
choices: Loading programs into memory and switching the CPU among them so many appear to run at once
Giving each program the illusion of its own private memory (virtualization)
Offering system calls such as `open()`, `write()` and `fork()`
Stopping one program from reading or corrupting another's memory
Translating C++ source into assembly
Physically storing bits as magnetized regions
questions.explain: The OS runs programs, virtualizes hardware, manages resources, provides system calls and enforces protection. Compiling is the job of a **compiler** (an application), and storing bits physically is the job of **hardware**.

questions.q: A game crashes, but your browser and the rest of the desktop keep running. Which OS role does this best illustrate?
choices: Protection
Hardware abstraction
Standard library of services
Compilation
questions.explain: **Protection** keeps one program's failure or misbehaviour from reading or corrupting another's memory and files, so one crash does not take down the whole system.

questions.q: A C++ program writes "hello world" to a file. How does the data get to the disk?
choices: The program makes system calls (`open`, `write`, `close`); the OS's file system works out where the data goes and issues I/O requests to the storage device
The program writes the bytes directly into the SSD's controller registers
The compiler stores the text in the executable, which the disk copies at boot
The CPU's control unit decides which block to use on its own
questions.explain: Applications request OS services through **system calls**. The OS routes file operations to its file system, which picks disk locations and issues the device I/O. Even saving a Notepad file triggers this hidden chain.

questions.q: Which component loses its contents when power is removed?
choices: Main memory (DRAM)
An SSD
A hard disk
A USB flash drive
questions.explain: RAM is **volatile**: it holds the programs and data currently in use, and is fast, but its contents vanish without power. Secondary storage (SSD, HDD, flash) is non-volatile. (Caveat 2 applies: non-volatile memory like Optane exists, and DRAM fades over seconds, not instantly.)

questions.q: Inside the CPU, which part performs addition and Boolean operations like AND/OR?
choices: The ALU (arithmetic logic unit)
The control unit
The system bus
The I/O bridge
questions.explain: The **ALU** does arithmetic and logic. The **control unit** directs the fetch–decode–execute cycle, **registers** are small fast storage cells, and **buses** are shared wires carrying addresses, data and control signals between parts.

questions.q: What is a **bus** in computer hardware?
choices: A shared group of wires carrying addresses, data and control signals between components
A program that moves files between folders
A type of non-volatile memory
The OS component that schedules processes
questions.explain: The system bus has address, data and control lines connecting the CPU, main memory and the I/O bridge/controllers.

questions.q: In the lesson, "hardware" one step above raw materials refers to…
choices: Organized components: CPU, main memory, secondary storage, I/O devices with controllers, and buses
Only the metal case and the plastic keyboard
The operating system's drivers
Anything that stores data, including files
questions.explain: The slides describe the lowest layer as metal, rubber, plastic and electricity, but those materials are organized into standard components: CPU, RAM, storage, I/O devices (through controllers/adapters) and buses. Module 2 tours them.

questions.q: Why do computers represent signals with just two voltage states (high ≈ 1, low ≈ 0) instead of, say, ten?
choices: Two well-separated states are much easier to build reliably and to distinguish through electrical noise
Transistors physically cannot hold more than two voltages
Binary uses less memory than decimal for the same number
The C++ standard requires binary hardware
questions.explain: With only two states you can leave a wide margin between them, so noise rarely flips a 0 into a 1. Ten levels packed into the same voltage range would be much closer together and error-prone. Module 1 revisits *why binary*.

questions.q: What is a transistor, in the terms of this lesson?
choices: A tiny electrically controlled switch: a voltage on one terminal decides whether current flows between the other two
A logic gate that computes AND
A small memory cell that holds one byte
A wire that carries data between the CPU and RAM
questions.explain: Transistors are the switches from which everything is built: a few make a **logic gate**, gates make adders, multiplexers and flip-flops, and those make ALUs, registers and a whole CPU.

questions.q: Using the truth table, what is the output of `(A AND B) OR (NOT A)` when A = 0 and B = 1? (Enter 0 or 1)
questions.explain: A AND B = 0 AND 1 = **0**. NOT A = NOT 0 = **1**. Then 0 OR 1 = **1**.

questions.q: Adding two 1-bit numbers A = 1 and B = 1 with sum = `A XOR B` and carry = `A AND B` gives…
choices: sum = 0, carry = 1, i.e. binary `10` = 2
sum = 1, carry = 1, i.e. binary `11` = 3
sum = 1, carry = 0, i.e. binary `01` = 1
sum = 0, carry = 0, i.e. binary `00` = 0
questions.explain: 1 XOR 1 = 0 (the bits are equal), and 1 AND 1 = 1, so the result is carry 1, sum 0 → `10`₂ = 2. Chaining 32 or 64 such adders with carries passed along gives an ALU's integer adder.

questions.q: Which chain correctly describes how hardware is built up?
choices: Transistors → logic gates → adders/multiplexers/flip-flops → ALUs and registers → CPU
Logic gates → transistors → CPU → ALUs → registers
Flip-flops → transistors → gates → buses
CPU → ALU → gates → transistors
questions.explain: It is layered abstraction again, in hardware: switches make gates, gates make functional circuits (adders, multiplexers, memory cells), and those combine into the processor.

questions.q: For a NOT gate, an input of 1 produces an output of 1.
questions.explain: NOT inverts its input: NOT 1 = 0 and NOT 0 = 1.

questions.q: A classmate says, "When I write C++ I'm talking directly to the hardware." Which facts from this module contradict that?
choices: The editor or IDE is itself an application written by someone else, running on the OS
C++ is a human-readable language designed by others that the hardware cannot run directly
The code must be preprocessed, compiled, assembled and linked by other programs, then loaded by the OS
Printing output goes through library code and an OS system call
C++ source is executed by the CPU one line at a time
questions.explain: Every step between your text and the CPU is software someone else wrote: the editor, the language design, the tool chain, the loader and the OS's system calls. The CPU only executes **machine code**, never C++ source.

questions.q: Which statement about language levels is correct?
choices: Assembly is roughly one line per machine instruction and is tied to a specific CPU family's instruction set
High-level languages are tied to one specific CPU
Machine code is human-readable mnemonics like `mov` and `ret`
Assembly runs on any CPU without changes
questions.explain: High-level code (Python, C++) is portable and must be translated. **Assembly** is mnemonics for one CPU family's instructions. **Machine code** is the raw bytes (e.g. `48 89 df`) the CPU decodes.

questions.q: How does standard Python (CPython) run your program?
choices: It compiles source into intermediate bytecode, then interprets that bytecode in a virtual machine
It compiles the whole program ahead of time into a native executable, like g++
The CPU executes Python source directly
The OS translates Python line by line into assembly on disk
questions.explain: A **compiler** (e.g. for C/C++) translates the whole program ahead of time to machine code; you run the executable. An **interpreter** carries out the program step by step as it runs. CPython does both: source → bytecode, then interprets the bytecode. Either way, another program sits between your code and the hardware.

questions.q: Put the Hello World build pipeline in order.
choices: Preprocessor → compiler → assembler → linker → loader (OS)
Compiler → preprocessor → linker → assembler → loader
Preprocessor → assembler → compiler → loader → linker
Linker → compiler → preprocessor → assembler → loader
questions.explain: `hello.cpp` → (preprocess) `hello.ii` expanded source → (compile) `hello.s` assembly → (assemble) `hello.o` object code → (link with libraries) `hello` executable → (OS loader) running process. Each arrow is a program someone else wrote.

questions.q: Running `g++ -E` on the 10-line Hello World produces about 45,000 lines. Why?
choices: `#include <iostream>` is replaced by the full contents of the iostream header and everything it includes
The preprocessor unrolls the `cout` statement into machine code
The linker adds the whole C++ standard library as source
Comments are expanded into documentation
questions.explain: The **preprocessor** handles `#` directives before real compilation. `#include` pastes in the header's text, which declares `std::cout`, `std::endl` and the rest of stream I/O, so the source grows enormously.

questions.q: What does the **linker** do in the pipeline?
choices: Joins the object file with library code (like the C++ standard library) to produce a runnable executable
Converts assembly mnemonics into machine-code bytes
Expands `#include` directives
Loads the program into memory and starts it
questions.explain: The assembler makes `hello.o` (machine code); the **linker** combines it with libraries into an executable (here a 16 KB ELF 64-bit file); the **OS loader** puts it in memory and runs it.

questions.q: The Hello World machine code contains `mov $0xd,%edx`. What is `0xd` in decimal?
questions.explain: Hex D = 13 (binary 1101). It is the length of `Hello, world!`: 5 + 1 (comma) + 1 (space) + 5 + 1 (!) = **13**. The compiler worked out the length ahead of time to pass to the output routine.

questions.q: When the running Hello World finally prints, how does the text reach your terminal?
choices: Library code for `cout` makes a `write` system call, and the OS sends the bytes to the terminal
The CPU writes pixels to the screen directly from `main`
The linker embedded the text into the terminal program
The preprocessor printed it during compilation
questions.explain: Output goes through the C++ library and then an OS **system call** (`write`). The program never touches the display hardware itself.

questions.q: Which of these are **IDEs** (not just text editors)?
choices: Visual Studio
CLion
Eclipse
Notepad
Nano
questions.explain: An IDE bundles an editor with build/compile, debugger, error highlighting, code completion and project management (Visual Studio, CLion, Code::Blocks, Eclipse, PyCharm). Notepad, Nano and Vim are plain text editors. Either way, it's an application at the top of the stack.

questions.q: The slides' Hello World contains `using namespace std` on its own line. What happens when you compile it with g++?
choices: It fails: the line is missing its semicolon, and g++ reports `expected ';' before 'int'`
It compiles and prints Hello, world!
It compiles but crashes at runtime
It fails because `main` must return `void`
questions.explain: `using namespace std` needs a terminating `;`. The fix is `using namespace std;`.

questions.q: Why does g++ point at `int` on the line *after* `using namespace std` rather than at the end of that line itself?
choices: The compiler reports where it *noticed* the problem: it expected `;` and found `int` instead
Line numbers in g++ are off by two
`int` is not allowed at the start of a line
The preprocessor moved the line
questions.explain: Parsers only know a `;` is missing when they hit the next token that can't continue the statement. So compiler errors often point just *after* the real mistake, a useful debugging habit to remember.

questions.q: What does `using namespace std;` do?
choices: Lets you write `cout` instead of `std::cout` by bringing standard-library names into scope
Includes the iostream header
Declares `main` as the entry point
Links the standard library into the executable
questions.explain: The C++ standard library lives in the **namespace** `std`, a named scope that prevents name clashes. The directive pulls those names into scope. It's common in teaching code but discouraged in large programs and headers because it imports *every* `std` name.

questions.q: What is the difference between `endl` and `'\n'`?
choices: `endl` inserts a newline **and flushes** the stream; `'\n'` only inserts the newline, so it's usually faster
`'\n'` flushes the stream; `endl` does not
They are identical in every way
`endl` ends the program
questions.explain: Flushing forces buffered output out immediately, which costs time. Prefer `'\n'` unless you need the flush.

questions.q: What happens if you delete `return 0;` from `main` in the corrected program?
choices: Nothing changes: reaching the end of `main` has the same effect as `return 0;`
It fails to compile
The exit status becomes a random value
The program prints nothing
questions.explain: The C++ standard special-cases `main`: falling off its end is equivalent to `return 0;`. This rule applies **only** to `main`, not other functions returning `int`.

questions.q: After running the corrected `./hello`, what does `echo $?` print?
questions.explain: `return 0;` hands 0 to the OS as the **exit status**. By convention 0 means success and non-zero means failure; `$?` shows the last command's status.

questions.q: `#include <iostream>` is an example of a…
choices: Preprocessor directive, handled before compilation proper
Linker flag
System call
Namespace declaration
questions.explain: Lines starting with `#` are handled by the **preprocessor**, which replaces this one with the text of the `<iostream>` header (declaring `std::cout`, `std::endl`, etc.).

questions.q: Why does every C++ program need `int main()`?
choices: Execution starts at `main`, and its `int` return value is reported to whoever started the program (the OS or shell)
It tells the preprocessor which header to include
It is required only by IDEs, not by g++
It declares the `std` namespace
questions.explain: `main` is the program's entry point, and its return value becomes the process's exit status.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say there is **no perfect definition** of a computer?
choices: Any sharp definition either excludes things we call computers or includes things we don't, so the word is defined by typical characteristics
Because computers change model numbers every year
Because the word "computer" was only coined in 1946
Because only electronic devices with an OS count, and that changes by vendor
questions.explain: Borderline devices pass some tests and fail others (cash registers, player pianos, pocket calculators). The slides say modern computers **tend to** have five characteristics, a checklist rather than a rule.

questions.q: For most of history, what did the word "computer" refer to?
choices: A person employed to perform calculations by hand or with simple tools
A mechanical adding machine
An electronic vacuum-tube machine
A punched-card loom
questions.explain: "Computer" was a job title: e.g. the Harvard Observatory's human computers, WWII ballistics teams computing firing tables, and NACA/NASA's computer pools (Katherine Johnson). The meaning moved to machines when machines took over the job.

questions.q: Why did the U.S. Army fund ENIAC?
choices: Human computers could not calculate artillery firing tables fast enough; one trajectory took a person about 20 hours
To replace the Harvard Observatory's star catalogs
To run the first web server
To tabulate the 1890 census
questions.explain: The Ballistic Research Laboratory fell far behind on firing tables. ENIAC did a trajectory in seconds, and six of the women computers became its first programmers.

questions.q: Which are among the five characteristics modern computers **tend** to have?
choices: Operate automatically
Perform arithmetic/logical operations
Store, process and retrieve data
Programmable
Electronic
Connected to the Internet
Have a graphical user interface
questions.explain: The five: **automatic, arithmetic/logical, store/process/retrieve data, programmable, electronic**. Network connectivity and GUIs are common but are not part of the list.

questions.q: A player piano plays music from a punched roll, and swapping the roll changes the piece. Why is it still not normally called a computer?
choices: It is mechanical/pneumatic rather than electronic, does no arithmetic or logic on data, and its roll cannot make decisions (no conditional branching)
Because it doesn't operate automatically
Because the roll is not a sequence of instructions at all
Because it was invented after the cash register
questions.explain: It is automatic and the roll resembles a program, but it fails the electronic and arithmetic/logic tests and is fixed-function: it can only play notes in order, with no "if this, then skip ahead."

questions.q: A mechanical cash register adds sales, stores a running total and displays it, all automatically. Which checklist items does it clearly **fail**?
choices: Programmable and electronic
Operates automatically and performs arithmetic
Stores data and operates automatically
It passes all five
questions.explain: It automatically does arithmetic (addition only) and stores a running total, so it "arguably" computes. But it's gear-driven (not electronic) and can only add up sales (not programmable/general-purpose).

questions.q: What is the key idea of the **stored-program (von Neumann)** architecture?
choices: Program instructions and data are kept in the same memory, so changing the job means loading different instructions
Programs are set by plugging patch cords and switches
The program is stored on a separate read-only punched roll
Data is stored only on disk, never in memory
questions.explain: ENIAC was originally programmed by rewiring, which took days. A stored-program machine changes jobs by loading new instructions into memory. Nearly every modern computer works this way, and it's why software is "stored as data."

questions.q: What does it take for a machine to be **general-purpose** (Turing complete) in practice?
choices: Conditional branching (decisions) plus the ability to read and write an unbounded amount of memory
A clock speed above 1 GHz
An operating system and a GUI
Being electronic rather than mechanical
questions.explain: Turing completeness means able to simulate a universal Turing machine, i.e. compute anything computable given enough memory. Babbage's mechanical Analytical Engine design was general-purpose; a piano roll, lacking branching, falls far short.

questions.q: Applying the five-item checklist, a smartphone is…
choices: A computer: it passes all five tests
Borderline, because it's not a desktop
Not a computer, because it's fixed-function
Not a computer, because it's not programmable
questions.explain: A smartphone is automatic, does arithmetic/logic, stores and retrieves data, is programmable (it runs arbitrary apps) and is electronic. People often forget it's a computer.

questions.q: A pocket calculator is electronic, automatic and does arithmetic. Which characteristic makes it *usually* not called a computer?
choices: It is essentially fixed-function, not programmable/general-purpose
It isn't electronic
It can't do arithmetic
It doesn't operate automatically
questions.explain: It's fast and electronic, but it does one kind of job. The checklist shows why the line between "computer" and "device" is a judgment call.

questions.q: Against the checklist, why is a 1940s human computer not a computer in the *modern* sense?
choices: It is not automatic and not electronic, though it does arithmetic, stores data on paper and follows procedures
It cannot perform arithmetic
It cannot store data
It cannot follow a procedure
questions.explain: The person does arithmetic, stores results on paper and follows written procedures (a kind of program), but a human is neither automatic in the machine sense nor electronic. It's the *original* meaning of the word.

questions.q: Which is the lesson's definition of a **computer system**?
choices: The set of components that work together to enable a computing device to function
A computer plus its monitor and keyboard
The operating system and its applications
Any network of two or more computers
questions.explain: A computer system is the set of cooperating components that let a computer function, and it has four kinds of component: **hardware, software, data and protocols**.

questions.q: Which are the four kinds of components of a computer system?
choices: Hardware
Software
Data
Protocols
Users
Electricity
questions.explain: Hardware (material components), software (instructions for the hardware), data (information and its physical form) and protocols (standards and procedures). Electricity is part of how hardware and data physically work, not a separate category.

questions.q: A printer's **device driver** is best classified as…
choices: Software (system software)
Hardware
Data
Protocol
questions.explain: Drivers are instructions that tell hardware what to do, part of system software along with the OS and utilities.

questions.q: The magnetized regions on a hard-disk platter that encode a file are best classified as…
choices: Data, in its physical form
Hardware
Software
Protocol
questions.explain: The platter itself is hardware, but the magnetization pattern *is* the file's data in physical form. The slide's phrase "(and its physical form)" is exactly this point.

questions.q: The USB specification is best classified as…
choices: Protocol (a standard)
Hardware
Software
Data
questions.explain: A specification is a set of agreed rules. It lets a USB stick from one company work with a laptop from another.

questions.q: A photo stored on your SSD is best classified as…
choices: Data
Hardware
Software
Protocol
questions.explain: Information present in the system is **data**. The SSD holding it is hardware.

questions.q: Why does the definition of a computer system include **protocols**, not just hardware and software?
choices: Independently built parts and machines can only cooperate if they follow shared rules (USB, PCIe/SATA, TCP/IP, HTTP)
Because protocols are a kind of hardware
Because only networked computers are computer systems
Because protocols store the operating system
questions.explain: Nothing in a computer works without agreed rules, even inside one box (PCIe, SATA, NVMe, ASCII/Unicode). Protocols also bridge to networking.

questions.q: Per Kurose & Ross, a protocol defines which of the following?
choices: The **format** of messages exchanged
The **order** of messages exchanged
The **actions** taken on sending/receiving a message or other event
The physical color of the cables
The programming language used to implement it
questions.explain: Format, order and actions. Human analogy: "Hi" → "Hi" → "Got the time?" → "2:00" has a format, a greeting-first order and an expected action (answer when asked).

questions.q: Which pairings of *where a bit lives* and *its physical form* are correct?
choices: DRAM: presence/absence of charge on a capacitor
Hard disk: direction of magnetization
Flash/SSD: charge trapped in a transistor's gate or charge-trap layer
Optical disc: pits vs. lands reflecting a laser
Fiber-optic cable: magnetized regions of glass
Wires and CPU logic: color of the insulation
questions.explain: Every bit must be a physical state: voltage (wires, logic), capacitor charge (DRAM, which must be refreshed), flip-flop state (SRAM), trapped charge (flash), magnetization (HDD), pits/lands (optical), light pulses (fiber), radio-wave modulation (Wi-Fi).

questions.q: Which of these is a protocol/standard for connecting components **inside** one computer?
choices: NVMe / PCI Express
HTTP
TCP
Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11)
questions.explain: PCIe, SATA and NVMe govern internal connections. HTTP and TCP are between programs over a network (IETF); Wi-Fi is local wireless networking (IEEE).

questions.q: Which best describes a **computer network**?
choices: Hosts connected by communication links and packet switches (routers, switches), exchanging data using shared protocols
The set of hardware, software, data and protocols in one computer
A single computer with many CPU cores
The OS's file system
questions.explain: A computer *system* makes one computer function; a *network* connects many systems. The Internet is a network of networks joined by IP. The NIC is just another I/O device, so protocols bridge the two halves of the course.

questions.q: Software is itself stored as data (for example, the machine-code bytes of a compiled program), which is the stored-program idea again.
questions.explain: Programs are just bytes in memory or on disk. That's why a stored-program computer can change jobs by loading different bytes.

questions.q: Which lists Modules 1–4 in the correct order?
choices: Binary & Hexadecimal → Tour of Computer Systems → Memory Hierarchy → Operating Systems
Tour of Computer Systems → Binary & Hexadecimal → Operating Systems → Memory Hierarchy
Operating Systems → Memory Hierarchy → Binary & Hexadecimal → Tour of Computer Systems
Binary & Hexadecimal → Memory Hierarchy → Tour of Computer Systems → Networking Essentials
questions.explain: 0 Class Intro, 1 Binary & Hex, 2 Tour of Computer Systems, 3 Memory Hierarchy, 4 Operating Systems, 5 Networking Essentials, 6 OSI Model / Network Stack, 7 High-Performance Computing. Modules 1–3 go *down* into data and hardware, 4 comes back *up* to the OS.

questions.q: How do Modules 5–7 relate to the abstraction stack?
choices: 5–6 go *outward* to connect machines, and 7 *scales up* to many machines working together
5–7 go further down into transistor physics
5–7 revisit binary notation
5–7 cover application programming
questions.explain: After a single system is understood (1–4), networking connects systems (5–6, with OSI/TCP-IP layering as another abstraction), and HPC combines many networked systems to compute in parallel (7).

questions.q: Which is an example of caveat 2, "virtually no statement is both useful and categorically true"?
choices: "An IP address identifies one computer," yet NAT puts many devices behind one address
"The world's fastest supercomputer changes every six months"
"We can't cover every aspect of networking in one course"
"C++ requires a semicolon after `using namespace std`"
questions.explain: Caveat 2 is about useful rules of thumb that have exceptions. Others: RAM is volatile (Optane), a byte is 8 bits (historically not always, hence "octet"), CPUs run instructions in order (out-of-order execution). The supercomputer example is caveat **3** (technology changes), and the coverage one is caveat **1**.

questions.q: The end of Dennard scaling around 2005 pushed the industry from ever-faster clock speeds to multicore CPUs. Which caveat does this illustrate?
choices: What is true today may not be true tomorrow
We must prioritize the major points
There is no perfect definition of a computer
Protocols define format, order and actions
questions.explain: "CPUs get faster clocks every year" was true until the power wall stopped it. Other expired facts: storage means spinning disks, there are enough IPv4 addresses (the IANA pool ran out in 2011).

questions.q: A detail seems glossed over in lecture. According to caveat 1, the most likely reason is…
choices: The field is enormous, so the course deliberately prioritizes major points and gives you the map, not every road
The detail is false
The detail is covered by the syllabus policies
Technology will soon make it obsolete
questions.explain: Each module is the subject of whole textbooks and graduate courses. An intro course teaches the major concepts, vocabulary and how pieces fit together.

questions.q: The word **tend** in "computers tend to have these characteristics" connects to caveat 2: the list is a typical-features checklist with exceptions, not a strict definition.
questions.explain: Both "no perfect definition" and "there is always an exception" express the same humility about sharp rules.

questions.q: "TCP guarantees delivery" is a useful statement. What is its exception?
choices: It guarantees reliable, ordered delivery *or* an error; if the link is cut, nothing is delivered
TCP never delivers data in order
TCP is a hardware component
TCP only works on Wi-Fi
questions.explain: A classic caveat-2 case: TCP provides reliability over an unreliable network where possible, but it can't beat physics. It reports failure rather than guaranteeing arrival.

questions.q: Which module (give the number) covers high-performance computing: parallelism, clusters and supercomputers?
questions.explain: Module 7 covers multicore CPUs, GPUs, clusters and supercomputers ranked by the TOP500 list (LINPACK/HPL, in FLOP/s). It builds on everything before it, since many networked systems compute together.
